title: Atomic Combinations: Molecular Structure

standard_text: Chemical bonds; Lewis diagrams of molecules; the VSEPR model and the shapes of molecules (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, bent); electronegativity and bond polarity; polar and non-polar molecules; bond energy and bond length. (summary of CAPS Physical Sciences, Grade 11, Chemistry: Atomic combinations: molecular structure)

key_big: Electron pairs repel and get as far apart as possible.
key_sub: A polar molecule has an uneven charge distribution.
body_html:
How to think about it

Atoms bond so that their outer energy levels are full. Lewis diagrams show bonding pairs and lone pairs. VSEPR: electron pairs around a central atom repel, which gives the shape: CO₂ linear, BF₃ trigonal planar, CH₄ tetrahedral, NH₃ trigonal pyramidal, H₂O bent (angular).

Electronegativity is the tendency of an atom to attract a bonding pair. A large difference (more than about 2,1) gives an ionic bond; a smaller difference gives a polar covalent bond. A molecule with polar bonds can still be non-polar if it is symmetrical, such as CO₂. Shorter bonds have higher bond energy.

Example

Shape of NH₃?

3 bonding pairs, 1 lone pair

Answer: trigonal pyramidal

Example

Is CO₂ polar?

It is linear and symmetrical.

Answer: no, it is non-polar

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting lone pairs when predicting shape.
  • Thinking a molecule with polar bonds is always polar.
  • Thinking electronegativity is the same as ionisation energy.

faq.q: Why is water bent and not linear?
faq.a: The two lone pairs on oxygen push the bonding pairs closer together.

faq.q: Which bond is more polar, H–F or H–Cl?
faq.a: H–F, because fluorine is more electronegative than chlorine.

items.q: How does a calcium atom (proton number 20) form an ion?
items.e: Atoms gain or lose electrons to reach a noble gas electronic configuration.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between copper (Cu) and sulfur (S)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of the Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion?
items.e: The ion has 10 electrons, the same arrangement as a noble gas.

items.q: Na<sup>+</sup> and N<sup>3−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 3 × (+1) + 1 × (−3) = 0.

items.q: What is the formula of the ion formed by aluminium?
items.e: Aluminium (Z = 13) loses 3 electrons.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between chlorine (Cl) and phosphorus (P)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of the Cl<sup>−</sup> ion?
items.e: The ion has 18 electrons, the same arrangement as a noble gas.

items.q: What is the formula of potassium oxide?
items.e: K<sup>+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is K<sub>2</sub>O.

items.q: What is the formula of strontium bromide?
items.e: Strontium forms Sr<sup>2+</sup> and bromine forms Br<sup>−</sup>; the charges must add to zero.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between nitrogen (N) and fluorine (F)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between aluminium (Al) and nitrogen (N)?

items.e: 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: tetrahedral.

items.q: Why do metals conduct electricity?
c: they have a sea of delocalised electrons that can move through the lattice
their ions move to the electrodes
items.e: Electrons carry the charge.

items.q: What is the bond angle in NH<sub>2</sub><sup>−</sup>?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs, 2 lone pairs. Lone pairs repel more than bonding pairs, so each lone pair closes the angle by about 2,5°.

items.q: What is the shape of H<sub>2</sub>S?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs around the central atom: bent (non-linear).

items.q: What is the shape of CO<sub>2</sub>?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: linear.

items.q: What does a high Rf value mean in paper chromatography?
c: the substance is more attracted to the mobile phase and moves further
the substance is insoluble in the solvent
the substance is more attracted to the paper
items.e: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent.

items.q: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points?
c: strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a lattice must be overcome
the covalent bonds inside molecules are strong
items.e: Every ion is attracted to many neighbours.

items.q: Why does ice float on water?
c: hydrogen bonds give ice an open structure that is less dense
items.e: Water is densest at 4 °C.

items.q: How many covalent bonds does fluorine (F) usually form?
items.e: It needs 1 more electrons for a full outer shell.

items.q: What is the shape of SF₆?
items.e: SF₆: octahedral.

items.q: Electronegativity: germanium (Ge) = 2,01 and chlorine (Cl) = 3,16. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 1,15. Below 0,4: nonpolar; 0,4–1,7: polar covalent; above 1,7: ionic.

items.q: In a bond between nitrogen (N) and carbon (C) (electronegativities 3,04 and 2,55), which atom gets a partial negative charge?
c: Neither; the electrons are shared equally.
items.e: The more electronegative atom pulls the shared electrons closer.

items.q: In a bond between bromine (Br) and hydrogen (H) (electronegativities 2,96 and 2,20), which atom gets a partial negative charge?
c: Neither; the electrons are shared equally.

items.q: Which substance would dissolve best in water?

items.e: ‘Like dissolves like’.

items.q: In a bond between chlorine (Cl) and germanium (Ge) (electronegativities 3,16 and 2,01), which atom gets a partial negative charge?

items.q: What does the kinetic molecular theory say about gas particles?
c: they all move at the same speed
they move randomly and rapidly, and their mean kinetic energy depends on temperature
items.e: Collisions with the walls cause pressure.

items.q: Why does hexane not dissolve in water?
c: hexane is non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water
items.e: Water molecules attract each other more strongly.

items.q: Why is ice less dense than liquid water?
c: ice contains air bubbles in every case
hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice
items.e: So ice floats and lakes freeze from the top.

items.q: Which molecule can form hydrogen bonds with other molecules of itself?
items.e: H must be bonded to N, O or F.

items.q: Why does a gas behave less ideally at high pressure?
c: the particles are close together, so their own volume and attractions matter
items.e: Ideal gases have no volume and no attractions.

items.q: Electronegativity: bromine (Br) = 2,96 and nitrogen (N) = 3,04. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 0,08. Below 0,4: nonpolar; 0,4–1,7: polar covalent; above 1,7: ionic.

items.q: Why is water's boiling point (100 °C) much higher than that of H₂S (−60 °C)?
c: water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other
items.e: H₂S has only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces.

items.q: Which temperature scale must be used in gas law calculations?
c: any scale, as long as it is the same throughout
the scale printed on the thermometer

items.q: Why is CO₂ a non-polar molecule even though its C=O bonds are polar?

items.e: Molecular shape decides overall polarity.

items.e: Boyle's law: pV is constant.
